rows.title: Correlation can change when you need it
scenario: Two hypothetical assets moved in opposite directions in three earlier observations. In a fourth observation both fall. A learner calls the fourth pair impossible because the assets were “uncorrelated.” The small sample cannot establish a permanent relationship, and low historical correlation does not promise that losses will offset in every interval.

Add the following hypothetical paired percentage moves: first observation A +2%, B −1%; second A −2%, B +1%; third A +1%, B −0.5%; fourth A −3%, B −4%. Treat them as a tiny illustrative sample rather than a permanent relationship estimate. Compare the direction pairs, then test an equal-dollar $1,000 holding in each asset for the fourth observation only.

rows.question: Does three earlier observations establish a permanent correlation?
